brief.question: How does the desktop design app talk to a cutting machine (over Bluetooth serial at 00:06:66:8d:2b:fe), and what core features (canvas, shapes/text/images, mat preview, materials, cut) must a Linux-friendly rebuild provide?
brief.purpose: Interoperability: build the person's own design-and-cut app that runs on Linux (Bazzite) and drives their own Maker machine.
brief.done_when: app/ builds, supports designing on a mat and sending to the machine over a Bluetooth RFCOMM/serial link with the documented protocol facts, plus --screenshot.

plan.title: Review the existing app and machine notes
Build and test the app
plan.why: Windows build, 22 tests, Linux compilation, and screenshot passed. Live pairing and cut streaming remain open.

findings.statement: Machine link framing (CricutDevice.exe): each message starts with a 2-byte big-endian header; top bit = encrypted, low 15 bits = payload length (max 512). Encrypted payloads are AES-256 ECB in 16-byte blocks; before encryption the payload is zero-padded to (len - len%16)+16 bytes and the last byte is set to the 8-bit sum of all bytes before it. Responses echo the command opcode as the first byte.

Maker-family ("Athena") command opcodes read from each command class's opcode getter: ClearError 0x0A, ReadErrorSeverity 0x0B (severity 0-3), SetSpeedState 0x31, SetToolState 0x37, SetFullToolState 0x3E, CPRToggle 0x3F, AbortCutting 0x68, GetInterfaceState 0x73, GetPersistentValueCount 0xA4, ScanForEdgeFloat 0xE2, BluetoothAlert 0xE5, HomeTheta 0xF0, Move4D 0xF1 (payload: opcode, axis mask 0x17, then big-endian float32 x, y, z, theta in radians), SendZeros 0xFF. Connection is Bluetooth RFCOMM serial (bluetooth_serial_transport, Windows.Devices.Bluetooth.Rfcomm).

The encrypted-session request (opcode 0xC7) is 51 bytes: plain header 00 31, code C7, a key slot chosen as random%12+2, then 47 random bytes; the slot selects one of 12 keys built into the original helper program. This also confirms plain frames use the same 2-byte length header with the top bit clear.

MatCraft's machine behaviour was measured by running its own framing, encryption, reply-reader, command-payload and mat-layout code and compared with the mechanics sheet and with the installed original's CricutDevice.exe bytes: 29 values match, 0 differ, 5 are estimates, 2 are not decoded. All 15 command codes, the Move4D mask 0x17, the degree constant 0.017453292519943295, the encrypted flag 0x80 and the 512-byte reply limit were read from the original file and agree.

The real machine on USB (COM6, 20D3:0015) answered three read-only commands (get interface state 0x73, read error severity 0x0B, get persistent value count 0xA4) with plain 2-byte-header replies whose first body byte is the command code, matching the mechanics sheet; the full behaviour check shows 38 same, 0 different, 6 estimates, 2 not yet.

Per a Hackaday article (xssfox), the machine sends its serial number to the PC software in plaintext over USB and the deactivation lock is enforced host-side (the software refuses serials on a disabled list), not in firmware; the encrypted cut packets are AES-ECB. MatCraft reads and shows the USB serial, keeps no activation list (so a maker-deactivated machine still works), and deliberately does not spoof another machine's serial.
The NewAES reply parser at 0x4f9180 accepts a big-endian reply length of 48 bytes and copies the reply into the command object. Its body does not derive the session key.

handoff: USB and Bluetooth Connect now send a read-only interface status request and require the matching reply before reporting connected. USB background readers stop after disconnect. Linux cargo build and all 23 tests passed; rebuild_check passed build and screenshot. No live hardware verification was performed in this run. Bluetooth on Bazzite, automatic key derivation and cut streaming remain open.
